newsitem.title: BULGARIA: BULGARIA'S JOINING NATO HINGED ON SPEEDY REFORM.
newsitem.headline: BULGARIA'S JOINING NATO HINGED ON SPEEDY REFORM.

text.p: U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen said on Monday Bulgaria had strong chances of joining NATO in future rounds of enlargement as soon as it overhauled its crisis-torn economy and Soviet-style military force.

Wrapping up an eight-day tour of Hungary, Ukraine and Bulgaria to assure Eastern European democracies that NATO remained open to more new members after inviting Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic to join in 1999, Cohen told reporters at Sofia airport:

"The decision in Madrid was a clear signal that as long as Bulgaria continues on its current path...of establishing strong civilian control over the military and reforming its military to bring it up to NATO standards, it will be a very strong contender for admission in the future rounds."
Cohen, President Bill Clinton and Secretary of State Madeleine Albright embarked last weeik on a post-Madrid diplomatic shuttle to explain U.S. policy on expansion of the alliance.

The secretary made no immediate promise of concrete additional U.S. military funds for Bulgaria's Soviet-style armed forces and did not say when Bulgaria, one of the staunchest Soviet allies during the Cold War, might be ready to join the alliance.
The Madrid summit named Slovenia and Bulgaria's northern neighbour, Romania, as possible front-runners for membership in the future.
"It is difficult to carry out quick changes in the army, but we are determined to launch and complete these reforms," said Georgi Ananiev, the country's first civilian defence minister.

The first step will be to downsize the military force by cutting conscription service to 12 months from current 18, Ananiev said. The move will meet NATO's requirement to reduce troops from around 95,000 now to some 65,000 in a year, said a defense ministry spokesman.
A new Defense and Armed Forces bill, yet to be passed by parliament envisages transforming the current army of conscripts into a professional one.
Ananiev did not say how long will it take cash-strapped Bulgaria to reform its army to NATO standards.
But after meeting top Bulgarian officials, Cohen said he was impressed with their determination to carry out military and economic reforms.
Bulgaria is considered a key state in the Balkan region because of its central position, sharing common borders with Greece, Turkey, Macedonia, Romania and Serbia.
"Bulgaria has strategic importance to Europe and the U.S. and can contribute greatly to stability in the entire region," said Cohen.
Praising the reformist government for rescuing the economy from a grave crisis earlier this year, Cohen urged Bulgaria to persist with free-market reforms and respect for human rights.

The United States currently provides about $6 million in military aid annually to Bulgaria, including funds to support the country's active participation in NATO's "Partnership for Peace" defence cooperation programme.
Cohen said it was important for NATO candidates first to focus on revamping their army communications control and English language training and then on new fighter jets.
"NATO will be open to all countries that measure up to its very high standards," said Cohen on departure to Washington.
